# The Ashwind tide cycle — field notes, part 2

The tide of the Ashwind Sea is semidiurnal: two high waters and two low waters
per tidal day. The tidal day is 24 h 50 min long, so every high water arrives
about 50 minutes later than the one on the previous day.

## Basic quantities

- tidal range R = height of high water minus height of low water
- mean range: 3.4 m at Torvig Harbour
- spring range: 5.1 m
- neap range: 1.7 m

The spring range is exactly three times the neap range at Torvig. The tide
office in Fenmouth uses this as its rule of thumb for the whole archipelago,
although Ovray Cove is known to deviate by up to 0.4 m.

## The rule of twelfths

Between low water and high water the water rises in six hours, and the rise per
hour is not constant. The tide office teaches the twelfths: 1/12, 2/12, 3/12,
3/12, 2/12, 1/12 of the range in the six successive hours.

Half the range is therefore reached after three hours, and the fastest rise is
in hours three and four.

## Spring and neap

Spring tides occur two days after new moon and two days after full moon, so
twice in a synodic month of 29.5 days. Neap tides fall between them, at the
quarters. The two-day lag is called the age of the tide.

## The Ovray rule

Ovray Cove dries out at any water level below 1.2 m above chart datum. Since
low water at springs is 0.3 m and at neaps 1.6 m, the cove is unreachable at
low water springs and usable throughout the neaps. Boats bound for Ovray Cove
plan their arrival within two hours either side of high water.

## Chart datum

All heights on the charts of the archipelago are given above chart datum, which
is the lowest astronomical tide. Soundings are therefore a worst case: the real
depth is almost always greater than the chart says.
